blocks.text: Some agent tasks cannot be finished in one exchange, no matter how good the model is. Migrating a large codebase, crawling a big set of documents, or monitoring a pipeline for days are jobs that spread across hours or days of real world time.
That changes what the agent needs underneath it. It is no longer enough to keep a plan in memory and hope the process never stops.
This lesson looks at what it takes to build an agent that can survive a restart, keep working from where it left off, and let a human see what it is doing right now.
1. What Makes an Agent Long Running

blocks.alt: A user submits a multi day task and the agent works in chunks, saving checkpoints

blocks.text: A long running agent is one whose task takes far longer to finish than a single interactive turn ever could. Instead of seconds, its work is measured in hours or even days.
The defining feature is not how smart the agent is, it is that the task outlives the conversation that started it.

items: Migrating a large codebase file by file across an entire weekend
Crawling and summarizing thousands of documents over several days
Watching a data pipeline and reacting to failures as they happen, indefinitely
Running a multi stage research task that needs to wait on slow external systems

blocks.text: 2. From Long Running Sessions to Long Running Agents

The earlier lesson on long running sessions looked at this problem from the conversation side, how context keeps growing turn after turn, and how compression and checkpointing keep that conversation usable.

This lesson looks at the same underlying pressure but from the agent side instead. The question is not just how the conversation stays healthy, it is how the agent itself keeps track of what it was doing.

A session can be kept alive and well compressed, and an agent running inside it can still lose its actual task the moment the process behind it dies, unless the agent layer is checkpointed on its own terms.
3. Why One Conversation Turn Is Not Enough
A normal chat exchange resolves in seconds, the model answers and the turn ends. A task that needs days of work simply cannot be squeezed into that shape.
Once work stretches across hours or days, interruptions stop being rare edge cases and become something you should expect. Deploys happen, servers restart, hosts reboot, networks drop.

blocks.title: Assume the interruption will happen
blocks.content: Anything that can interrupt a process, a deploy, a crash, a restart, a network blip, will eventually happen during a task that runs for days. Design for that from the start rather than treating it as a rare exception.

blocks.text: 4. The Shape of a Long Running Agent Task

blocks.alt: A long running task spans many chunks of work over extended time

blocks.text: A long running agent task usually has the same basic shape. There is one overall goal, broken down into an ordered list of steps, and the agent works through those steps one at a time.
Some steps finish in seconds, others might take minutes or hours, especially when they wait on slow external systems or large amounts of data.

code.content:
task = {
    "goal": "Migrate all API routes from v1 style handlers to v2 style handlers",
    "plan": [
        {"step": 1, "description": "List every v1 route file in the repo"},
        {"step": 2, "description": "Convert routes in batch one"},
        {"step": 3, "description": "Run the test suite against batch one"},
        {"step": 4, "description": "Convert routes in batch two"},
        {"step": 5, "description": "Run the test suite against batch two"},
        {"step": 6, "description": "Open a summary pull request"},
    ],
    "current_step": 1,
}

blocks.text: 5. Why These Agents Cannot Live In Memory Alone
If a plan and its progress only exist as variables in a running process, they vanish the moment that process stops, whether that is a crash, a redeploy, or just the machine restarting.
For a task that finishes in a minute, that risk barely matters. For a task that runs across days, treating memory as durable storage is a bug that is only waiting for the right moment to show itself.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Where state lives","Survives a restart","Visible to a human mid task"],"rows":[["In memory only","No","No"],["Written to a database as a checkpoint","Yes","Yes"]]}

blocks.text: 6. What a Checkpoint Actually Contains

blocks.alt: A checkpoint captures progress, remaining steps, and accumulated state

blocks.text: A checkpoint is a snapshot of everything the agent would need to pick its task back up exactly where it left off, written somewhere that outlives the process.

items: The original goal, in enough detail to reconstruct intent
The full ordered plan, not just the current step
Which step is the last one confirmed complete
Any partial results or intermediate output produced so far
A timestamp showing when the checkpoint was last updated

blocks.text: 7. Designing the Plan So It Can Be Checkpointed
A plan that is one giant opaque call cannot be checkpointed in any useful way, because there is no smaller unit to mark as done.
A plan built from discrete, ordered steps with a clear finish line for each one gives the agent something concrete to record progress against.
Every step should also have a way to tell whether it actually finished, not just whether the agent believes it finished.
8. Writing a Checkpoint to a Database
Saving a checkpoint is simply writing the current plan and progress to durable storage, keyed by a task id so it can be found again later.

code.content:
import json
import time

def save_checkpoint(db, task_id, task):
    db.checkpoints.update_one(
        {"task_id": task_id},
        {"$set": {
            "task_id": task_id,
            "goal": task["goal"],
            "plan": task["plan"],
            "current_step": task["current_step"],
            "results": task.get("results", {}),
            "updated_at": time.time(),
        }},
        upsert=True,
    )

# called after every step finishes, not just at the very end
save_checkpoint(db, "migrate-v1-to-v2-42", task)

blocks.text: That single call is the difference between an agent that disappears on restart and one that can be found again.
9. Detecting a Restart and Loading the Checkpoint

blocks.alt: A restart is detected and the last checkpoint is loaded back

blocks.text: When a new process starts, the very first thing a long running agent should do is check storage for any task that was left unfinished, before starting anything fresh.
10. Resuming Work From Where It Left Off

blocks.alt: Work resumes exactly where the last checkpoint left off

blocks.text: Once the checkpoint is loaded, the agent simply continues its loop from the recorded current step instead of step one.
Steps before the recorded current step are simply skipped, because the checkpoint already says they are done.
11. Idempotency: Avoiding Repeated Side Effects on Resume

blocks.alt: A resumed step avoids repeating a side effect it already completed

blocks.text: The tricky part is not the steps that finished cleanly, it is a step that was halfway through a side effect, like sending an email or writing a file, when the process died.
If the checkpoint marks that step complete only after the side effect is confirmed, a resume will simply redo the step, which can duplicate the effect.

blocks.title: Design steps to be safe to repeat
blocks.content: Give side effecting steps an idempotency key, or check whether the effect already happened before repeating it. A migration step should check whether a file was already converted before converting it again.

blocks.text: 12. How Often to Checkpoint

Checkpointing after every single tiny action adds overhead and slows the agent down for little benefit. Checkpointing only at the very end defeats the whole point, since a crash five minutes before completion would lose everything.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Checkpoint frequency","Risk on crash","Overhead"],"rows":[["After every step","Low, at most one step is redone","Small and steady"],["Only at the end","High, the entire task restarts from scratch","None until the end"],["On a fixed timer, every few minutes","Moderate, bounded by the timer interval","Low and predictable"]]}

blocks.text: For most agents, checkpointing right after each step finishes is the simplest rule that still keeps risk low.
13. Giving Humans Visibility Into Current Status

blocks.alt: A status view gives humans visibility into current agent progress

blocks.text: A person watching a long running agent should not have to wait until it finishes, or fails, to find out what it is doing. They should be able to check in at any moment.

items: What the current step is, in plain language
How many steps are done out of the total plan
When the last checkpoint was saved
Any partial results produced so far
Whether the agent appears stuck, based on how long it has been on the same step

blocks.text: 14. Building a Simple Status View
Because every checkpoint already lives in a database, a status view is often just a read of the same record the agent writes to.
No separate reporting system is required, the same checkpoint that lets the agent resume also lets a human check in.
15. Failure Modes Specific to Long Running Agents
Long running agents fail in ways that short lived ones rarely do, mostly because there is so much more time for something to go quietly wrong.

items: The agent gets stuck on one step and nothing ever notices, since there is no final answer to wait for
The world changes underneath a stale plan, like a file being deleted after the plan already assumed it exists
A restart replays a side effect that already happened, because the step was not written to be safe to repeat
Cost quietly grows far larger than expected because nobody set a limit on total steps or total run time

blocks.text: 16. Testing a Long Running Agent's Recovery Path
The recovery path is not something to hope works, it is something to actually test, the same way you would test any other critical code path.
A simple test is to kill the process partway through a task on purpose, then start a new process and confirm it resumes from the right step, with no side effect repeated.
If that test is never run, the first real test of the recovery path will be a real crash, in production, on a task that actually mattered.
Worked Example
Picture an agent tasked with migrating two hundred API route files from an old style to a new style, a job expected to take most of a day.
It builds a plan with one step per batch of twenty files, six batches total, and checkpoints after each batch finishes.

code.content:
task_id = "migrate-v1-to-v2-42"
task = load_checkpoint(db, task_id) or build_fresh_task()

run_task(db, task_id, task)
# if the process is killed partway through batch four,
# the next process to start simply calls load_checkpoint,
# sees current_step is 4, and continues from batch four,
# skipping the three batches already converted

blocks.text: Partway through batch four, the server hosting the agent gets redeployed and the process dies. A new process starts, loads the checkpoint, sees three batches are already done, and picks up batch four without redoing any earlier work.
A team lead checking the status view at that moment sees three of six batches done and a timestamp from a few minutes earlier, enough to know the task is healthy and moving.
Common Mistakes

items: Keeping the plan and progress only in memory, with no durable record anywhere.
Checkpointing only at the very end, so a late crash loses the entire task.
Marking a step complete before confirming its side effect actually happened.
Building steps that are not safe to repeat, so a resume can send a duplicate email or write a file twice.
Giving humans no way to see progress until the task fully finishes or fully fails.
Never actually testing the restart and resume path before relying on it in production.

blocks.text: Practice
Take the six step migration plan from the worked example and write your own version of save_checkpoint and load_checkpoint using a plain dictionary in place of a real database.
Then simulate a crash by stopping your loop halfway through the plan, call load_checkpoint again, and confirm the resumed run skips the steps already marked done.
Key Takeaway
A long running agent needs its plan and its progress written somewhere durable, not just held in memory, because a task spanning hours or days will almost certainly outlive at least one restart.

Checkpointing that state after each step, designing steps to be safe to repeat, and exposing the same checkpoint as a human readable status view turns a fragile background job into one people can trust and actually watch.
